## Proof

**Answer: Yes.** The spectral norm $\|J_f(x)\|_2 \le M$ holds for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. In fact, the symmetry hypothesis on the Jacobian is not needed — the bound follows from Lipschitzness and differentiability alone.

---

Since $J_f(x)$ is assumed to exist (and be symmetric) for every $x$, the map $f$ is differentiable everywhere. Fix an arbitrary point $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and an arbitrary unit vector $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $\|v\|_2 = 1$.

For every $t \neq 0$, applying the $M$-Lipschitz condition to the pair $(x, x + tv)$ gives

$$
\|f(x + tv) - f(x)\|_2 \;\le\; M\,\|tv\|_2 \;=\; M\,|t|.
$$

Dividing by $|t|$,

$$
\left\|\frac{f(x + tv) - f(x)}{t}\right\|_2 \;\le\; M, \qquad \text{for all } t \neq 0.
$$

The norm is continuous, so taking the limit $t \to 0$ and using the differentiability of $f$ at $x$ (which gives $\frac{f(x+tv)-f(x)}{t} \to J_f(x)\,v$) yields

$$
\|J_f(x)\,v\|_2 \;\le\; M.
$$

This holds for **every** unit vector $v$. Taking the supremum over all such $v$,

$$
\|J_f(x)\|_2 \;=\; \sup_{\|v\|_2 = 1} \|J_f(x)\,v\|_2 \;\le\; M.
$$

Since $x$ was arbitrary, $\|J_f(x)\|_2 \le M$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

---

**Remark on the symmetry hypothesis.** The conclusion uses only that $f$ is $M$-Lipschitz and differentiable at $x$. The symmetry of $J_f(x)$ (equivalently, that $f$ is locally a gradient field) plays no role in the argument. For a symmetric Jacobian, the spectral norm coincides with the largest absolute eigenvalue $\max_i |\lambda_i(J_f(x))|$, so the result can be restated as: every eigenvalue of $J_f(x)$ lies in $[-M, M]$. This is a strictly stronger-looking statement that nonetheless follows from the same one-line Lipschitz estimate above.

### PROOF COMPLETE
